title: From Legacy Machine Learning to Generative AI
author: Charlie Connor · Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source reframes AI from a threat to expertise reproduction as a tool that can accelerate learning and make training easier. It still calls for firms to redesign professional development, but does not endorse the cluster’s competence paradox or its claim that automation may erode the experiential basis needed for verification; its support is explicitly anecdotal and predictive.

kp.d: Connor contrasts legacy machine-learning work requiring a month of model training and examples with current demonstrations producing contract summaries, topic extraction and document citations during client calls without training data. He describes Harvey Vault generating typed fields and export context conversationally, replacing field, layout and view configuration that previously took two days in Relativity. cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Charlie Connor argues that generative AI radically accelerates contract analysis, shifts legal-tech value toward workflows and usable outputs, and creates opportunities for agentic automation, lawyer augmentation and changes to discovery.
pts.d: Connor makes several distinct claims. First, contract extraction and analysis that previously required model training and substantial configuration can now be performed during client calls without task-specific training data. Harvey Vault can create typed fields and exportable results through questions rather than manual setup. Second, new entrants without accumulated technical debt can rapidly build credible products, while familiar platforms risk becoming unnecessarily cumbersome; he questions conventional CLM purchasing in favor of an AI-first toolkit organized around business priorities. Third, he locates potentially investible value in application and agentic workflows rather than answer generation alone: systems could classify documents, suggest fields, run OCR and organize review so humans can interpret results rather than merely check outputs. Fourth, AI can help professionals prepare, explore counterarguments and identify gaps in their thinking. He frames employment risk primarily as failure to learn the tools, not straightforward elimination of all jobs. Fifth, AI can support proactive regulatory and commercial intelligence that previously required multiple teams and databases. Finally, generative AI is already being applied in eDiscovery; he expects first-pass responsiveness review to be automatable with human quality control, and predicts retrieval systems will increasingly work with data where it resides. He speculates that better information could change litigation behavior and make organized, explainable diligence materials an expectation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Connor mainly supports his claims with firsthand product-development experience, demonstrations, client work and team feedback, rather than formal performance or labor-market evidence.
pts.d: Connor contrasts his experience building Heretic and working at Relativity with current demonstrations and consulting work at Gravity Stack. Examples include a maritime-company diligence call, an SLA-analysis demonstration retrieving topics and citations from approximately 2,000 documents, Harvey Vault's field-generation and export features, and NewCode's architecture and model-selection demonstration. He reports showing clients results from seven tools using the same documents and questions; this is practical comparative evaluation, not a reported standardized benchmark. For eDiscovery, he reports approximately nine projects on a product transcribed as 'air' and favorable team feedback, but supplies no measured accuracy, review-cost or time-saving results. His employment, investment, litigation-behavior and future diligence claims are judgments or possibilities, not findings established by the examples. He also invokes an unspecified Microsoft observation about efficiency versus thinking and an unspecified Harvard Business Review account of increased litigation and judicial-clerk hiring. These are secondhand references without study details, and the historical eDiscovery example functions as an analogy rather than evidence of generative AI's future effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Connor describes contract-analysis improvements and eDiscovery deployments as current in early 2025, while presenting agentic workflows, in-place retrieval and downstream market changes as emerging possibilities without firm deadlines.
pts.d: The conversation situates current capabilities in early 2025 and compares them with legacy machine-learning development over roughly the preceding decade. Connor describes viable products built since 2023, live client-call analysis and natural-language export creation as already available. He treats automation of first-pass review as an active industry objective associated with 2025, not as a fully demonstrated universal replacement for review. In-place retrieval, broader agentic orchestration and changed diligence expectations are forecasts. Adoption is conditional on useful workflows, sensible expectations, appropriate prompts, portable outputs and avoiding information overload. He explicitly notes imperfect citations and continued human quality control. Rapid change also makes multiyear technology commitments unattractive to him. He repeatedly emphasizes uncertainty about ultimate consequences rather than supplying a determinate forecast of employment or litigation volumes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are lawyers and associates, corporate contract stakeholders, litigation service providers, legal-tech vendors and the consultants helping buyers choose tools.
pts.d: Transactional lawyers and contract-review teams can obtain structured answers and summaries faster, while partners and other recipients may continue to prefer spreadsheets over entering specialist software. Associates and experienced lawyers gain preparation and counterargument support; Connor favors recruiting associates who use tools effectively and suggests commercially relevant regulatory analysis as a developmental task. His warning about job loss concerns professionals who fail to acquire tool competence, with no quantified displacement estimate. Corporate legal teams share contract-system interests with sales, support and senior leadership, making business priorities and ownership important to an AI-first approach. Litigation reviewers and service providers face automation of first-pass work and potential cannibalization of existing services, while humans still check results. Established vendors face technical-debt and workflow disadvantages; startups can build quickly but must supply useful application layers and exports. Gravity Stack's stated role shifts toward comparing available tools on client materials and helping clients interpret the differences. Litigants and transaction participants could eventually face changed information advantages and expectations for diligence readiness. Connor does not make a specific access-to-justice claim about unmet civil legal need.
